'''Naum Il'ich Feldman''' (26 November 1918 – 20 April 1994) was a Soviet mathematician who specialized in number theory.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Korobov|first=N M|last2=Nesterenko|first2=Yu V|last3=Shidlovskii|first3=A B|date=1995|title=Naum Il'ich Feld'man (obituary)|url=http://www.numbertheory.org/obituaries/RMS/feldman/index.html|journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys|volume=50|issue=6|pages=1247–1252|doi=10.1070/rm1995v050n06abeh002639|issn=0036-0279|bibcode=1995RuMaS..50.1247K|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>Yu V Nesterenko and A B Shidlovskii, "In memory of Naum Il'ich Feldman [1918-1994]" (in Russian), ''Vestnik Moskovskogo Universiteta. Seriya 1. Matematika. Mekhanika'' (6) (1995), 108-109.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Feldman|first=Naum|date=2000|title=Algebraic and transcendental numbers|url=http://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV10N6.pdf|journal=Quantum|volume=10|issue=6|pages=22–26}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=Nesterenko|first=Yu. V.|chapter=Hilbert's Seventh Problem|date=2006|title=Mathematical Events of the Twentieth Century|pages=269–282|editor-last=Bolibruch|editor-first=A. A.|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|language=en|doi=10.1007/3-540-29462-7_13|isbn=978-3-540-29462-7|editor2-last=Osipov|editor2-first=Yu. S.|editor3-last=Sinai|editor3-first=Ya. G.|editor4-last=Arnold|editor4-first=V. I.|editor-link4=Vladimir Arnold}}</ref>

== Life ==

Feldman was born on 26 November 1918 in [[Melitopol]], [[Zaporizhia Oblast]] of southeastern [[Ukraine]].

He entered in 1936 the Faculty of Mathematics and Mechanics at the [[University of Leningrad]] where he specialized in number theory under the supervision of [[Rodion Kuzmin|Rodion O. Kuzmin]]. After his graduation in 1941, Feldman was called up by the army and served from October 1941 until the end of the World war II. For his service, he was awarded the [[Order of the Red Star]], the [[Order of the Patriotic War]] (second class), and the medals [[Medal "For the Capture of Königsberg"|"For the Capture of Königsberg"]], [[Medal "For the Defence of Moscow"|"For the Defence of Moscow"]], [[Medal "For the Victory over Germany in the Great Patriotic War 1941–1945"]].<ref name=":0" />

After his demobilization, he started his PhD in 1946 at the Institute of Mathematics at the University of Moscow, under the supervision of [[Alexander Gelfond|Alexander O. Gelfond]], and he presented his Ph.D. thesis in 1949. In 1950, he became head of the Department of Mathematics of the [[Ufimsky District|Ufimsky]] Oil Institute, where he was assigned until 1954. He lectured at the [[Russian State Geological Prospecting University|Moscow Geological Prospecting Institute]] from 1954 to 1961.<ref name=":0" />

From September 1961 Feldman worked at Moscow State University, first in the department of mathematical analysis, and then in the department of number theory. In 1974 he became Doctor of Science. Feldman got full professorship in 1980.<ref name=":0" />

Feldman died on 20 April 1994.

== Work ==
Feldman obtained important results in number theory. His main research area were the theory of [[Diophantine approximation]]s, the theory of [[transcendental number]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fel'dman|first=N I|last2=Shidlovskii|first2=A B|date=1967|title=The Development And Present State Of The Theory Of Transcendental Numbers|journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys|volume=22|issue=3|pages=1–79|doi=10.1070/rm1967v022n03abeh001219|issn=0036-0279|bibcode=1967RuMaS..22....1F}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Transcendental Numbers|url=https://archive.org/details/numbertheorytran00pars|url-access=limited|last=Feldman|first=N. I.|last2=Nesterenko|first2=Yu. V.|date=1998|publisher=Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-540-61467-8|editor-last1=Parshin|editor-first1=A. N.|series=Number Theory IV|pages=[https://archive.org/details/numbertheorytran00pars/page/n145 146]–147|editor-last2=Shafarevich|editor-first2=I. R.}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|url=http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=im&paperid=3636&option_lang=eng|title=The measure of transcendency of the number <math>\pi</math> |last=Feldman|first=N. I.|journal=Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat.|volume=24|issue=3 |year=1960|pages=357–368}}</ref> and [[Diophantine equation]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Feldman|first=N. I.|date=1970|title=Effective bounds for the number of solutions of certain diophantine equations|journal=Mathematical Notes of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR|language=en|volume=8|issue=3|pages=674–679|doi=10.1007/BF01159064|issn=1573-8876}}</ref>

In 1899, French mathematician [[Émile Borel]] strengthened the famous theorem of [[Charles Hermite]] that proved in 1873 the transcendence of the number {{math|[[e (mathematical constant)|e]]}} without having been specifically constructed for this purpose. Later different estimates of the measure of transcendence were considered for other numbers too. Feldman's mentor Gelfond obtained his most famous result in 1948 in his [[Gelfond's theorem|eponymous theorem]], also known as the [[Hilbert's seventh problem|7th Hilbert's problem]]:<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=0486495264|title=Transcendental and algebraic numbers|last1=Gel'fond|first1=A. O.|publisher=[[Dover Publications]]|year=1960|isbn=978-0-486-49526-2|series=Dover Phoenix editions|location=New York|mr=0057921|orig-year=1952}}</ref>

: If α and β are [[algebraic number]]s (with α≠0 and α≠1), and if β is not a [[Real number|real]] [[rational number]], then any value of α<sup>β</sup> is a [[transcendental number]].

In 1949, Feldman further improved Gelfond's method to estimate of the measure of transcendence for logarithms of algebraic numbers and periods of elliptic curves.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fel'dman|first=N I|date=1968|title=Improved Estimate For A Linear Form Of The Logarithms Of Algebraic Numbers|journal=Mathematics of the USSR-Sbornik|volume=6|issue=3|pages=393–406|doi=10.1070/sm1968v006n03abeh001067|issn=0025-5734|bibcode=1968SbMat...6..393F}}</ref>  Of special importance is his result from 1960 on the measure of the transcendence of the number <math display="inline">\pi</math>.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />
